competitors.title: LangGraph Interrupts Documentation
key_points: interrupt() function pauses graph execution and returns value to caller; requires checkpointer + thread_id
Resume with Command(resume=...) using same thread_id; node restarts from beginning of interrupted node
Event streaming (v3 API) surfaces interrupts via stream.interrupts and stream.interrupted
Common patterns: approval workflows, review-and-edit state, tool-level interrupts, multiple parallel interrupts
Interrupt payloads can be any JSON-serializable value; resume values become return of interrupt() call
Multiple interrupts in parallel branches can be resumed simultaneously with resume_map mapping interrupt IDs to values
Tool-level interrupts let approval logic live with the tool itself, reusable across graph parts
Checkpointing saves exact graph state so execution can resume later, even from error states

competitors.title: How we built a persistent agent memory layer on Elasticsearch with 0.89 recall and zero tenant leaks
key_points: Three-index memory architecture: episodic (events), semantic (facts), procedural (playbooks) with different lifecycles
Hybrid retrieval pipeline: RRF over BM25 + Jina v5 dense, then cross-encoder reranker on merged candidates
80 candidates per retrieval leg, RRF with rank_constant=30, Jina v2 cross-encoder reranker
Time-decay scoring: gauss-shaped multiplier with 180d flat offset and 1825d (5yr) half-life scale
Use-count boost: 1 + log10(1 + use_count) * 0.2 for frequently recalled facts
Supersession pattern: old facts hidden via superseded_by filter, audit trail preserved, ILM archives to cold storage
DLS (Document-Level Security) for multi-tenant isolation: per-user API keys with DLS queries enforced server-side
R@10 0.89 across 168 questions with zero cross-tenant leaks; semantic facts hardest (R@10 0.81), episodic 0.98, procedural 1.0
Consolidation LLM promotes episodic events into semantic facts and procedural playbooks every turn
MCP endpoint for any agent client (Claude Desktop, Cursor) to use same memory layer

competitors.title: Your search index is already an agent memory system: Persistent agent memory for Claude Code with Elasticsearch
key_points: agent-memory project: bridge CLI with 7 Elasticsearch indices (agent-memory, agent-messages, agent-tasks, agent-sessions, agent-status, entities, entity-history)
Three Claude Code hooks: SessionStart (sync-memories + heartbeat), PostToolUse (entity index-file on .md writes), Stop (session-end log)
Hybrid recall with ES|QL FUSE (RRF, k=60) for memory; FUSE LINEAR (0.3 BM25 / 0.7 semantic) for entity graph search
BRIDGE_MEMORY_DECAY_WINDOW default 45d half-life for temporal decay
Offline queue: writes go to fallback/outbox/ as JSON files when ES unreachable, flushed via bulk API on reconnect
Knowledge graph layer: entities from markdown frontmatter (initiative, blocked_by, depends_on), depth-2 traversal
Cross-device memory: shared ES index as source of truth, bridge sync-memories on SessionStart
bridge graph commands: search, related, check-blockers, semantic-diff, gen-handoff, reconcile
Production instance: 533 memories, 50,802 sessions, 207 entities, 1,364 relationship edges

competitors.title: Systematic research with LangChain's Deep Agents framework and Elasticsearch
key_points: Deep Agents is LangChain's agent harness built on LangGraph: write_todos, task delegation, file I/O, persistence
Five-step research pipeline: Plan (write_todos), Research (sub-agents with web_search + store_finding), Evaluate (aggregate findings), Review (cross-check), Explore (Agent Builder)
Structured findings in ES with metadata: research_angle, evidence_type, relevance_score, source_credibility
semantic_text field with Jina v5 embeddings auto-generated at index time via copy_to pattern
Sub-agents have isolated context windows; orchestrator context stays clean while specialists do deep work
Agent Builder provisioned programmatically at pipeline end for team exploration via Kibana UI
Mentions HITL approval gates: 'Add human-in-the-loop approval gates using LangGraph's interrupt pattern'

competitors.title: Extract chart data standard OCR misses: Elastic Agent Builder and LlamaParse in one pipeline
key_points: LlamaParse Extract: schema-driven extraction returning structured JSON from PDFs including chart/visual data
Elastic Workflows tool chains: upload PDF → create extraction job → poll until done → index → verify
ES|QL tools for structured queries (numeric filters) and narrative text search (MATCH on text fields)
Agent Builder agents with workflow tools + ES|QL tools for end-to-end document processing
Pydantic schema defines extraction fields; descriptions serve as instructions to extraction model
19 iterations max (~3 min cap) for LlamaParse extraction polling

angles: Build production HITL agents with LangGraph + Elasticsearch — combine interrupt() for human oversight with ES for persistent memory across sessions
Three memory types for agentic workflows — episodic (events), semantic (facts), procedural (playbooks) each with different lifecycles and retrieval strategies
Hybrid retrieval beats pure semantic for agent memory — BM25 catches exact references (task IDs, version numbers) while dense vectors handle conceptual matches
Multi-tenant isolation with DLS — security-first agent memory where isolation lives in the cluster, not in application filters
From research to production with HITL gates — Deep Agents pipeline with interrupt-based approval gates for critical actions
Cross-device agent memory — bridge CLI and shared ES indices let agents recall context across machines without git pull
Schema-driven document extraction for agents — LlamaParse Extract + ES|QL tools for structured data from complex PDFs
The interrupt pattern as a first-class primitive — dynamic interrupts (not static breakpoints) for approval, review-and-edit, and tool-level oversight
Offline-first agent memory — fallback queue writes to local JSON when ES unreachable, bulk-synced on reconnect
outline: Introduction — Why HITL matters for production agent systems in 2026
LangGraph HITL Fundamentals — interrupt(), Command(resume=...), checkpointer, thread_id, event streaming v3
Common HITL Patterns — approval workflows, review-and-edit state, tool-level interrupts, multiple parallel interrupts
Elasticsearch as Agent Memory Backend — three-index architecture (episodic/semantic/procedural), lifecycle management
Hybrid Retrieval for Agent Memory — BM25 + Jina v5 dense + RRF fusion + cross-encoder reranker
Time-Decay and Use-Count Scoring — gauss-shaped decay, 180d flat offset, 5yr half-life, frequency boost
Multi-Tenant Isolation with DLS — per-user API keys, server-side enforcement, shared catalog integration
Supersession and Audit Trails — handling contradictions, superseded_by pattern, ILM cold storage archiving
Cross-Device Memory with bridge CLI — seven indices, three Claude Code hooks, offline queue, knowledge graph
Building a Complete HITL Agent Pipeline — Deep Agents orchestrator with interrupt-based approval gates
Schema-Driven Document Extraction — LlamaParse Extract + Elastic Workflows + ES|QL tools
Production Considerations — scaling, monitoring, schema evolution, fallback strategies
Conclusion — When to use LangGraph + ES for HITL agents vs purpose-built solutions
